tagline: Lakes, rocky ridges and the head of the Bedford Basin
lines: Bedford takes its name from the 4th Duke of Bedford, colonial secretary in 1749.
The Mi'kmaq call this area Kwipek, and ancient petroglyphs here are a National Historic Site.
Fort Sackville was built here in 1749 by Gorham's Rangers, the year Halifax was founded.
Until the mid-1850s, this whole area went by the name Sackville.
Scott Manor House dates from 1770 and still hosts a tea party during Bedford Days.
Around 1819 a paper mill on the Basin made paper for the Acadian Recorder newspaper.
In the 1930s the Moirs chocolate company moved part of its factory to Bedford.
Bedford became a town in 1980, then joined the Halifax Regional Municipality in 1996.
The Bedford Basin is about 8 km long and up to 71 m deep, fed by the Sackville River.
In both world wars, merchant convoys gathered in the Basin before crossing the Atlantic.
DeWolf Park honours a Bedford native: Canada's most decorated naval officer of WWII.
A waterfront boardwalk of about 1 km runs through DeWolf Park toward Shore Drive.
The Chickenburger on the Bedford Highway is said to be Canada's oldest drive-in diner.
The Larry Uteck interchange on Highway 102 opened in 2010 to serve new Bedford suburbs.
known_for: DeWolf Park and the waterfront boardwalk
Many lakes: Paper Mill, Kearney, Sandy, Marsh
history: Ancient: Mi'kmaq presence for thousands of years; petroglyphs now a National Historic Site
1749: Gorham's Rangers build Fort Sackville at the head of the Basin
1752: George Scott receives a large land grant near the fort
c. 1819: Anthony Holland opens the Acadian Paper Mill on the Basin
1930s: Moirs moves part of its chocolate factory to Bedford
1980: Bedford is incorporated as a town, with Francene Cosman as first mayor
1996: Bedford becomes a community within the Halifax Regional Municipality

Tea party at Scott Manor House
rhythm: Bedford sits about 18 km from downtown Halifax, linked by the Bedford Highway and Highway 102, so its roads fill with traffic heading in and out of the city. Summer peaks with Bedford Days around Canada Day in DeWolf Park, while each winter the Light Up Bedford Parade rolls along the Bedford Highway from Bedford Place Mall to the waterfront, on the Sunday after Halifax holds its own parade.
